newsitem.title: BURMA: Suu Kyi group vows calm after attack on motorcade.
newsitem.headline: Suu Kyi group vows calm after attack on motorcade.

text.p: Burma's opposition National League for Democracy (NLD) party said on Sunday it would not be provoked by an attack on its leader Aung San Suu Kyi's motorcade.
NLD vice-chairman U Tin Oo said that Saturday's attack, the first of its kind against Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi, was a new tactic by the ruling military government to intimidate her.
Suu Kyi was unhurt by the stones thrown at her motorcade but outraged by the attack and said it was government orchestrated.

"...we will not stir up any counter reaction by the people because what has happened is politically favourable to us," U Tin Oo told Reuters before leaving for a meeting with Suu Kyi and other top NLD party leaders on Sunday.
People could see from the incident who the provocateurs were, and it was not the NLD, he added.
A government official said investigations were under way to find out who had carried out the attack.

Suu Kyi, whose car windshield was smashed by stone-throwers, was travelling in a motorcade to meet hundreds of supporters near a police checkpoint barring public access to her University Avenue residence.
U Tin Oo's car windows were also smashed, as were those of two government security cars also in the motorcade.
Suu Kyi and U Tin Oo had complained on Saturday that uniformed security personnel at the scene failed to deter the attackers.
"The whole thing was carefully orchestrated by the authorities. What kind of government is it that allows such hooliganism?" Suu Kyi said.
The stone throwers dispersed only after a government security officer in the motorcade waved his pistol in the air.
U Tin Oo said the NLD believed that the attackers were obviously from townships outside Rangoon and were brought into the capital to cause the disturbance.
He said Suu Kyi, who met her supporters just after the incident, had refrained from telling them about it so as to not stir up emotions.
Most Rangoon residents were unaware of the incident as the official media did not mention it on Sunday.
U Tin Oo said: "As a result of this attack, we can go back to the SLORC and say we did not react, so let us have dialogue."
He added that despite the attack the NLD would not buckle and instead would use it to make political gain.
A government official said late on Saturday that the attackers must have been people fed up with Suu Kyi's political activities, particularly on weekends, which they found to be disruptive.
"She (Suu Kyi) thinks the whole country likes what she does, but there are some people who are fed up with her activities and dont like her," he added.

Suu Kyi and the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) have been engaged in a standoff over her demand for greater democracy in Burma since her release in July, 1995, from six years of house arrest.
The SLORC has detained and then released hundreds of her National League for Democracy (NLD) party supporters and members at various times to pressure her.
